p.title: Automatic construction of direction-aware sentiment lexicon using direction-dependent words

ext.title: Automatic construction of direction-aware sentiment lexicon using direction-dependent words
ext.venue: Language Resources and Evaluation, vol. 59, pp. 843-869 (accepted 28 Mar 2024; published online 25 May 2024)
ext.coverage: Read the full extracted text (all ~1,684 lines: front matter, abstract, Sections 1-6, Appendix 1, data/funding statements, references, author affiliations). Tables 1-9 were read from the extracted text, which garbles some table layouts; the numbers quoted below are as they appear in that text and should be checked against the PDF table before reuse. Paul's markup: no markup files were listed for this item, so paul_markup is empty. The _annots folder was not opened for this paper. Scope relevance: text measurement (lexicon construction, PMI co-occurrence, sentence classification) only. Nothing in the paper concerns lobbying, networks, path-finding, allocation, elections, persuasion/turnout, or legislators.
ext.research_question: Can a financial sentiment lexicon be built automatically so that each entry is a pair of a directional word (up/down) and a direction-dependent word, so that sentiment flips correctly with direction (e.g., "cost" negative, but "cost decrease" positive)? Does adding these pairs to the Loughran-McDonald (LM) word list improve sentence-level sentiment classification of financial headlines? (Sect. 1, pp. 845-846)
ext.theory: Lexicon-based explainability: sentiment lexicons are preferred in finance because they expose the words that drive a decision, whereas supervised deep models are black boxes (Sect. 1, pp. 845-846). Domain-specific polarity: a word's sentiment depends on domain and on directional modifiers. Direction-dependency is operationalized as a word whose sentiment orientation changes with "up" or "down" words (Sect. 1, p. 846; Sect. 3.1, p. 850). No formal economic theory is stated beyond the market-sentiment and media literature cited in the introduction (Tetlock 2007; Engelberg and Parsons 2011; Garcia 2013).
ext.data: Unit: sentence or economic news headline. Construction corpus: DS50 subset of the Financial PhraseBank (FPB), 4,835 English sentences labelled by 16 finance experts; 691 sentences tagged "proportional" and 28 tagged "inversely proportional" after the direction-score step; 56 direction-dependent words extracted; Senti-DD lexicon of 1,767 pairs (1,077 positive, 690 negative) (Sect. 4.1, p. 853; Table 1, p. 848). Evaluation corpora: FPB subsets DS50 (4,835), DS66 (4,209), DS75 (3,447), DS100 (2,259); SemEval-2017 Task 5 subtask 2 (960 messages, continuous scores converted to three classes); FiQA Task 1 (436 sentences) (Sect. 4.3, pp. 855-856; Table 6, p. 856). Directional word lists: 20 "up" and 11 "down" terms seeded from HGI word lists (Table 3, p. 853). Time period: not stated for the corpora; the appendix examples are dated roughly 2006-2010. Evaluation uses stratified five-fold cross-validation repeated five times (Sect. 4.3, p. 856).
ext.method: Stage 1 (direction tagging, Sect. 3.1): each polar sentence gets a direction score = count of "up" words minus count of "down" words (Porter stemming, NLTK). Sentences are tagged "proportional" (positive with score > 0, or negative with score < 0) or "inversely proportional" (the reverse). Neutral sentences are excluded. Stage 2 (association, Sect. 3.2): nouns are lemmatized (NLTK); nouns occurring in fewer than 1% of sentences are dropped. PMI(w,t) = log2 [p(w,t) / (p(w) p(t))] is computed for each noun and tag. Dependency score (Eq. 1) keeps PMI(w,tp) if PMI(w,tp) - PMI(w,ti) > delta, uses -PMI(w,ti) if the difference is below -delta, and 0 otherwise; delta = 0 in this study. Stage 3 (extraction, Sect. 3.3): from each sentence, the highest-scoring proportional word or the lowest-scoring inversely proportional word is kept as the direction-dependent word; words with non-alphabetic characters or fewer than k = 3 letters are removed. Stage 4 (Senti-DD, Sect. 3.4): pairs of directional and direction-dependent words are labelled positive-context or negative-context. Stage 5 (evaluation, Sect. 4.2): LM sentiment score = PosScore - NegScore (Eq. 2); ContextScore = ContPosScore - ContNegScore (Eq. 3); RefinedScore = SentimentScore + ContextScore (Eq. 4); sign of the refined score gives positive, neutral or negative. Baselines: Sentiment140, SentiWordNet, SO-CAL, MPQA, TextBlob, VADER, SentiStrength, AFINN, LM. Pretrained comparators: Word2Vec with logistic regression (word2vec-google-news-300), BERT-base-uncased and RoBERTa-base fine-tuned (Adam, weight decay 0.01, batch 8, 500 warm-up steps, 3 epochs; Sect. 4.4, pp. 856-857). Hyperparameters were set heuristically, and the authors state that tuning is left to future work (p. 857).
ext.identification: None in the causal sense. The paper does not identify any causal effect. Validity rests on the downstream classification F1 of the augmented lexicon against baselines, with the explainability of individual pairs checked by inspection (Appendix 1, pp. 863-866; Table 9, p. 861). The paper says that evaluating lexicon quality directly needs inter-annotator agreement that it did not collect (Sect. 4.2, p. 854).
ext.scope: Population: English-language economic and financial news headlines (FPB, SemEval-2017 Task 5, FiQA), mainly company-performance headlines from Finnish and other European firms that reflect the FPB corpus. Institution: Seoul National University (Industrial Engineering). Era: the corpora are dated to the mid-2000s to 2010s; the paper does not state a period for its sample. The method is claimed for other domains such as electronics reviews, and for central-bank communications (FOMC) as future work (Sect. 6, pp. 862-863). These extensions were not tested.

key_findings.finding: Senti-DD construction yields 56 direction-dependent words (49 proportional, 7 inversely proportional), e.g., proportional: profit, revenue, growth, net; inversely proportional: cost, plant, traffic.
The lexicon has 1,767 directional/direction-dependent pairs, 1,077 positive and 690 negative.
Worked PMI example for profit: PMI(profit, proportional) = 0.05 and PMI(profit, inversely proportional) = -3.0, giving dependency score 0.05.
key_findings.numbers: PMI 0.05 and -3.0; dependency score 0.05; 217 sentences contain profit

key_findings.finding: On the four FPB subsets, LM + Senti-DD raises weighted F1 over the LM list alone. The reported F1 values are DS50 0.5914 to 0.7057, DS66 0.6023 to 0.7322, DS75 0.6174 to 0.7788 and DS100 0.5982 to 0.8233. The paper says it beats all lexicon baselines.
On DS100, LM+Senti-DD roughly doubles the negative-class F1 of LM (text says nearly twice). Table values: negative F1 0.4087 (LM) to 0.7260; positive F1 0.2596 (LM) to 0.7361.

On the SemEval and FiQA sets, LM+Senti-DD is still below 0.5 F1 (0.4789 SemEval; 0.4937 FiQA). Pretrained models do better on nearly all measures, and the authors attribute this to lexicon methods needing explicit sentiment words.
key_findings.numbers: F1 SemEval LM 0.3632 -> LM+Senti-DD 0.4789; FiQA LM 0.3635 -> LM+Senti-DD 0.4937

key_findings.finding: The DS100 pretrained models score higher than LM+Senti-DD (e.g., RoBERTa F1 0.9620 on DS100 in the Table 7 text), so the lexicon does not reach state-of-the-art accuracy. The paper says this is an explainability trade-off.
key_findings.location: Table 7 p. 859; Sect. 5 p. 858; Sect. 6 p. 862
key_findings.numbers: RoBERTa DS100 weighted F1 0.9620 as extracted

key_findings.finding: Worked example: LM labels 'Profit for the period was EUR 10.9 mn, down from EUR 14.3 mn in 2009' neutral, but LM+Senti-DD labels it negative via the (profit, down) pair (refined score -1).
key_findings.location: Sect. 5 p. 857; Table 5 p. 855; Fig. 3 p. 858

key_findings.finding: In a 20-sentence DS100 sample, 10 predictions are correct and 10 are wrong. Failures mainly come from context pairs the lexicon counts as non-neutral, e.g., (company, increase).
Only 28 of 719 sentences in the construction corpus are inversely proportional, and this imbalance produces noisy direction-dependent words such as beer and day.

limitations: Directional word lists are chosen manually by the researchers, which the authors call time-consuming and subjective; the directional vocabulary may also go out of date (Sect. 6, p. 863).
Imbalance between proportional (691) and inversely proportional (28) tagged sentences yields noisy words such as beer and day (Sect. 5, p. 862).
Neutrality is detected passively (equal positive and negative counts), not by a dedicated neutrality step (Sect. 6, p. 863).
Lexicon methods degrade when sentiment is not explicitly expressed; SemEval and FiQA F1 stay below 0.5 (Sect. 5, p. 858).
Pretrained model inference is treated as black box; the paper's statements about why pretrained models succeed are speculative (Sect. 5, p. 858).
Hyperparameters, including the number of epochs and delta = 0, k = 3, were set heuristically; no hyperparameter tuning was done (Sect. 4.4, p. 857).
Evaluation relies on downstream classification F1 without inter-annotator agreement measures; the authors say lexicon quality is hard to assess directly (Sect. 4.2, p. 854).
Sentence-level only, English-only, and mostly headline-length texts; generalization to other domains (electronics reviews, FOMC minutes) is proposed but untested (Sect. 6, pp. 862-863).
Table 7 and Table 8 values in the extracted text are layout-garbled; the reported results have no significance tests or confidence intervals in the text read.
Appendix examples show the lexicon can flag a context pair (company, increase) as a negative cue, which reduces accuracy on some headlines (Sect. 5, p. 862).

short_quotes.quote: sentiment orientation of a word can change depending on the application of directional expressions

measures: Weighted precision, recall and F1 for three-class (positive/neutral/negative) sentence classification on FPB subsets, SemEval-2017, and FiQA
Per-class precision, recall and F1 (DS100, Table 8)
Pointwise mutual information PMI(w,t) between nouns and direction-dependency tags (p. 850)
references_of_note: Loughran and McDonald (2011), 'When is a liability not a liability?', Journal of Finance 66(1), 35-65: the LM word list used as base lexicon and the main manual financial lexicon.
Oliveira, Cortez and Areal (2016), Decision Support Systems 85: StockTwits lexicon built with modifier-association statistics; the closest prior work on directional modifiers (pp. 847, 848).
Malo, Sinha, Korhonen, Wallenius and Takala (2014), JASIST 65(4): Financial PhraseBank, and a manual lexicon of 177 entities combined with up/down motion verbs.
Moreno-Ortiz, Fernandez-Cruz and Hernandez (2020), SentiEcon, LREC: manual financial lexicon of 6,470 entries with directional multi-word expressions.
Krishnamoorthy (2018), Knowledge and Information Systems 56(2): manual lagging and leading performance-indicator lexicon (directional word lists).
Yekrangi and Abdolvand (2021), Journal of Intelligent Information Systems 57(1): PMI-based financial lexicon construction from Bloomberg and Reuters text.
Tetlock (2007), Journal of Finance 62(3); Engelberg and Parsons (2011), Journal of Finance 66(1): media and market sentiment, cited as motivation.
Taboada et al. (2011), Computational Linguistics 37(2): SO-CAL lexicon method used as a baseline.
Cortis et al. (2017), SemEval-2017 Task 5, and Maia et al. (2018), FiQA challenge: evaluation datasets.

rel.summary_md:
Park, Lee and Cho build a financial sentiment lexicon in which each entry pairs a directional word ("up" or "down" family) with a noun whose polarity depends on that direction. Their example is "cost", which is negative alone but positive in "cost decrease". Sentences in the Financial PhraseBank are tagged proportional or inversely proportional from an up-count minus down-count score. PMI between nouns and the two tags picks out 56 direction-dependent words, and these yield 1,767 pairs. Adding the pairs to Loughran-McDonald raises weighted F1 on the PhraseBank subsets from about 0.59-0.62 to 0.71-0.82. On SemEval and FiQA it stays below 0.5, and fine-tuned RoBERTa is far ahead (about 0.96 on DS100). The construction set was heavily imbalanced (28 inversely proportional sentences against 691 proportional), which produced noisy words. Evaluation covers headline-length sentences only, with no significance tests.

This paper has already been used in Paul's system. The brain notes say he adapted it as a "directional verb x CU-valenced target" override for the CFPB sign-flip problem. A whole-text version made 46 sign changes on gold: 3 good and 43 bad. It was rejected because releases defending the CFPB describe the attack with "shrink" verbs. The idea that survives in the built system is a curated, direction-separated target registry (cfpb_reform +1, cfpb_expansion -1, cfpb_institution 0), not an automatic lexicon. The paper explains both results. Its pairs work on short headlines where the direction word modifies the noun, and press releases are long, multi-actor texts. The paper's own failure cases (pairs like company/increase) and its class imbalance match the churn seen in Paul's dry run. The open question in the system (restrict the rule to the sentence or headline that names the bill) is the condition under which the paper's evidence would actually transfer. Nothing here concerns networks, money or allocation.

bearings.paper_claim: Direction-aware (directional word, direction-dependent word) pairs fix polarity flips like (profit, down), taking LM's neutral to negative. LM+Senti-DD weighted F1 is 0.7057-0.8233 on the FPB subsets, but on headline-length, single-actor sentences only. It stays below 0.5 on SemEval (0.4789) and FiQA (0.4937), and the 20-sentence error sample is 10/20 correct, with failures from spurious pairs such as (company, increase).
bearings.paper_location: Table 7 pp. 858-859; Table 5 p. 855; Sect. 5 pp. 857-862; Appendix 1 pp. 863-866
bearings.system_side: Sign comes from DEBATE or the human overlay for text-bearing releases, and from the bill table only for text-less billstatus rows (run_stage5.R:135-143). The naive directional-verb x target override adapted from this paper over whole release text gave 3 good / 43 bad sign changes on gold and was rejected. The 'defend the CFPB' releases describe the attack with shrink verbs, so the verb count reads the wrong direction. The brain note's recorded pivot is a high-precision headline or named-bill-only rule, or using the signal as a DEBATE feature rather than an override.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence carries over only when the directional word syntactically governs the target noun within one short sentence, as in FPB headlines. It does not carry over to whole-release counting over multi-actor congressional press text. There, the speaker's attitude toward the direction (defending vs attacking) is a second hop the paper never models. The paper's own domain shift (FPB to SemEval/FiQA) already drops F1 below 0.5. This supports the system's open question about restricting the rule to the sentence naming the bill. It does not support reviving a blanket override, and any such variant is UNVERIFIED until a held-out gold look.

bearings.paper_claim: Polarity is a property of a (direction, target) pair, not of the target alone. Direction-dependent nouns are typed proportional or inversely proportional by PMI against direction-tagged sentences (dependency score Eq. 1, delta = 0). Only 28 of 719 tagged sentences were inversely proportional, and the imbalance produced noisy entries such as beer and day.
bearings.system_side: Valence is attached per target family, with separate entries per direction: cfpb_reform +1, cfpb_expansion -1, cfpb_institution 0, cfpb_general 0. Families are derived from Paul's gold labels at at least 75% consistency, and the docstring records 'no flip heuristics (those failed)'. The brain note records a PMI auto-typing pass on gold (CFPB 64% inverse at sentence level vs 41% at release level). Auto-registry variants all fell below the flat baseline of 0.677, while the gold-derived registry reached 0.782 accuracy in 5-fold CV.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Paul's registry is in effect a hand-curated, gold-derived version of the paper's direction-pair lexicon, and the paper's automatic PMI step is the part that failed here. Two things are consistent with the paper's own imbalance warning. Inverse targets are a small minority on both sides, and the system's sentence-level typing beat release-level typing. Transfer is limited by corpus size: 400 tweet golds and 238 distinct targets, against the paper's 4,835 sentences with a 1% noun-frequency floor. A PMI typing pass on this corpus would also need a held-out look before any claim (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: General and finance dictionaries miss or misread polarity when sentiment is carried by direction plus noun. LM alone labels 'Profit ... down from EUR 14.3 mn' neutral (SentimentScore 0). On DS100, negative-class F1 for LM alone is 0.4087, against 0.7260 with direction pairs.
bearings.paper_location: Sect. 5 p. 857; Table 5 p. 855; Table 8 p. 860
bearings.system_side: LSD2015 counts are direction-blind word and negation-phrase sums. Press intensity = |net|/words (or charge) and is multiplied by the DEBATE or human sign, so LSD contributes magnitude only.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The bearing is weak because LSD's sign is discarded here. The paper's flips matter for sign, and for magnitude only when directional pairs cancel or inflate |net|. That happens in releases like 'cut costs / reduce fees', where an LSD negative word sits in a positive context. The paper tests no effect on intensity, and Paul's system has no human-coded intensity criterion to test it against.

gaps_exposed: No sentence- or headline-scoped direction rule. Every directional-lexicon test in the system counted over whole release text, while the paper's evidence is sentence-level and its pairs require the direction word to govern the noun.

No representation of speaker attitude toward the direction ('defend against efforts to dismantle the CFPB'). The paper does not model this either, and it is the dominant failure mode in Paul's dry run. A direction-pair feature would need dependency or clause scoping before it could help DEBATE.
The direction-pair signal was never tried as a soft feature into the stacked stance readers. That was the recorded pivot option, and it has no held-out measurement.
LSD intensity ignores direction-dependent polarity. Whether this distorts |net| on CU press releases is untested, and there is no human-coded intensity gold.
flags: The system has already tested and rejected this paper's method as adapted: naive directional-verb x target override, 3 good / 43 bad on gold. Do not re-propose a whole-text direction-aware override. Any sentence-scoped revival stays UNVERIFIED until a held-out gold look reproduces it (DE-062).

The paper's F1 values come from layout-garbled table text and have no significance tests or confidence intervals. Check them against the PDF before quoting, and attach the corpus and denominator, e.g. 'weighted F1 on FPB DS100, 2,259 sentences, 5x5-fold CV'.

The paper's domain (European company-performance headlines, mid-2000s to 2010s) is not congressional press. Its evidence does not transfer to the multi-topic releases that dominate the Stage 5 corpus.
rel.paul_alignment: There are no annotations, but Paul acted on the paper. He adapted it for the CFPB sign-flip problem (memory note cu-signflip-directionality; brain two-hop note). The built system agrees with the paper's core idea, that polarity belongs to the pair and not the word: the direction-separated CFPB families in derive_valence_registry.py are a hand-curated Senti-DD. It disagrees on automation, because the automatic and naive version churned (3 good / 43 bad), and the paper's own headline-only scope and class-imbalance warnings predict that. Paul's memory note's present-tense line ('user pursuing a direction-aware sentiment lexicon') is stale. That line of work ended in rejection of the override and the curated registry. The remaining live question is the sentence-scoped or feature-only variant.

related.why: Both build domain-specific sentiment dictionaries from corpus co-occurrence rather than general word lists. Rice & Zorn is the political-text analogue that the legacy regex scorer's polarity formula cites.
A dictionary approach for political communication validated with crowdcoding. It supplies the human-agreement lexicon check that Park et al. say they lack (Sect. 4.2).

Fine-tuned RoBERTa beats classical and lexicon methods on political stance, consistent with Park's own Table 7 gap (RoBERTa about 0.96 vs lexicon 0.82 on DS100). This favours the system's DEBATE reader over a lexicon override.
LLM position extraction (Support/Oppose) on lobbying reports is the transformer alternative to directional lexicons for bill-level sign. Paul ties it to bill-sign handling.
